title: Automatic referral triggers for early specialist palliative care in outpatient oncology: a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial
subtitle: Eight disease-site clinics switching from usual referral to opt-out triggers
statement: At a regional cancer centre, referral to specialist palliative care depends on the treating oncologist and comes late: in 2025 the median time from the first palliative care visit to death was 34 days, and a third of patients who died under the centre's care were never seen. The centre proposes automatic referral triggers in the electronic health record, with oncologist opt-out, and wants to test them against usual referral in a pragmatic trial in which its eight clinics switch to triggers in a staggered order.
whoAffected: Adults with advanced solid tumours and their families, the oncologists who would receive automatic referrals, and the palliative care team whose clinic capacity is limited.
whatHurts: Late or absent palliative care means that symptom support, care planning and family support arrive in the last weeks of life or not at all, and many patients spend their final month in hospital.
currentPractice: Referral at the oncologist's discretion, without criteria; no trigger or prompt in the electronic health record.
whyNow: Trigger rules can be built from early 2027, the medical oncology division has agreed to take part, and the palliative care team can add nurse time.
constraints: The palliative care team can add 0.5 full-time equivalent nurse time and no physician time. Trigger rules can be built in the electronic health record from the first quarter of 2027. Outcomes must come from routinely collected data; no extra questionnaires for patients who are very unwell.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients with advanced cancer spend more of their remaining time at home, with symptom support and care planning offered early enough to use.
summary: Problem framed as a pragmatic stepped-wedge trial of opt-out automatic referral triggers across eight clinics.
